items.title: Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Like Count Basie, there is the best example... Oh Basie was a master. Well Basie played with Benny you know on a couple of records.

ctx.x: Those are good words. We’ll put those in capitals.

No it is true. The same with an arrangement. If you’ve going to write an arrangement and all of a sudden the singer sings something, and you’ve got the whole band coming in, there’s no place for it to go. You’ve got to let the rhythm play first. Like Count Basie, there is the best example. They start —

items.title: Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 23, 2003 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: he just played in the cracks... the music of Count Basie, the rhythm section never played figures with the band.

ctx.x: How come? What was it about them?

Well you know when you have four rhythm, and you know what you’re doing, the guitar is the last guy to be hired and the first guy to be fired. But in Freddie Green’s case, without Freddie there’s no band. Because he gave that rhythm section — and Count Basie played sparingly, never overplayed, he just played in the cracks. And that’s the big difference.
Yeah. Is there some distinguishing thing about what Freddie Green did that’s possible to verbalize?

items.title: 52157_Count Basie oral history interview
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] ...when you each play heads where the solo's always set? Bucky, you take this chorus... Or was there ever a time when Buck wanted to take a chorus and it wasn't set ahead of time? [INTERVIEWEE] He just jumped in there without anybody knowing?

ctx.x: "That ain't like I heard it." You know? But if you just play an arrangement, naturally. (unintelligible) He's playing what he -- how he feels. He's playing (unintelligible) ad lib expecially a jazz solo.

Bucky, you take this chorus; you take this chorus; you take this chorus? Or was there ever a time when Buck wanted to take a chorus and it wasn't set ahead of time?
